prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery, by the Jarillo-Herrero group, of correlated insulating and superconducting states in this system, opening the field of moire quantum materials.

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B046) as my single-part position, and the exchange has made me more, not less, confident. The chair's central question is B046 against B041, and the round-1 statements show that both camps list the same weaknesses and differ only in weighting. My weighting rests on what each prize would recognise. B046 is a sharp prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) followed by a decisive observation (the Jarillo-Herrero group, 2018) that created a gate-tunable platform which many independent groups now use for correlated and topological phases. The first-round statements of Eriksson, Johansson and Olsson, who each state that they moved or kept B046 after reading all the openings, independently reach the same trio and near-identical wording, which tells me the credit is workable rather than contrived. I have changed one thing from round 1: the citation now says explicitly that the experimental discovery was made by the Jarillo-Herrero group, following Eriksson's request and Johansson's point that the citation should not settle the team's internal credit. The preferred configuration is otherwise unchanged. A two-part configuration such as B046 with B041 would need five different people, so it is excluded by the three-name limit, and I do not see a defensible pairing in any case.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is maturity. The discovery is about eight years old, the pairing mechanism is unresolved, and twist-angle disorder still limits reproducibility of the finer details. Attribution is also incomplete, since Yuan Cao as first author and the Dean, Yacoby and Young groups are outside the credit, and Santos and Peres earlier on twisted bilayers are not covered either. B041 is the more mature case with the cleaner credit, and B001 has three decades of testing. If a colleague holds that a prize should wait until the interpretation settles, that is a legitimate position and I cannot refute it with evidence, only with a different weighting of what the discovery consists of. Lindroth and Pearce are right that B041 is a strong prize; my disagreement is about which is the larger scientific step this year, not about its quality.

responses.point: Argues that B041 is mature, cleanly attributed and distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, with the 1e-18 result resting on understood atomic-structure shifts, and that I (and Mehlig) weigh B046 too lightly against it.
responses.response: I accept your argument on distinctness, and I said in round 1 that I do not regard the lattice clock as incremental to the comb prize. The magic-wavelength idea and the control of systematic shifts are real physics. We differ on weighting. A clock that is two orders of magnitude better than caesium refines a measurement we already knew how to make, while B046 gave the field a new tunable class of materials with phases nobody had observed in this form. I also note that the strong-reproduction argument you make for the clocks is the same one I make for the phases in B046, so I do not think maturity alone separates them. I move nothing, but I agree B041 deserves to be the first alternative.

responses.point: Moved from B033 to B041 on the grounds of cleanest attribution, independent reproduction and broad concrete reach, and describes B046 as held back by the open superconducting question and the uncredited first author.
responses.response: Your attribution point is fair and I conceded in round 1 that B041 is cleaner on credit. Where I disagree is the claim that the open question is about readiness. The prize would rest on the existence of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle, which many groups have measured, and not on the pairing mechanism, so the open mechanism does not undermine the cited achievement. I also appreciate that you moved off B033 for the same attribution reasons I gave, and that you offered to recuse on it. I keep B033 as a second alternative only because it is a discovery of nature, not because I think the two-name credit is solved.

responses.point: Lists B046 as first alternative, accepts that it is best supported, but says timing and credit for the experimental side make it a real judgement call and that lattice clocks are a distinct achievement.
responses.response: We are closer than the labels suggest. I agree the experimental allocation is a judgement call and I now put the Jarillo-Herrero group into the citation to reflect that. On timing, I think the committee should ask whether the discovery would change if the mechanism were settled in either direction, and the answer is no: the platform and the phases stand regardless. Your Hall-laboratory disclosure for B041 reads to me as ordinary professional proximity to a mentor and not a reason for recusal, but I leave that to the committee. If B041 became the principal proposal I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Keeps B001 (dynamical mean-field theory) as his configuration on conceptual originality and thirty years of confirmation, and ranked B046 eighth on maturity.
responses.response: I respect the maturity argument and I think B001 is the best-tested candidate on the table. My difficulty is the one you and Eriksson both raise. Metzner is outside the trio and it is open whether this is a discovery of nature or a method, and a finite-dimensional approximation cannot be called controlled in the sense a sceptic would expect. Those problems sit in the citation rather than in the science, and I do not see a three-name formulation that resolves them this year. I would not object to DMFT in a later year, as I said in round 1, and I note that you yourself no longer press B030, which I also doubted as a phenomenon.

responses.point: Moved B046 to the top and asks that the citation state that the discovery was made by the Jarillo-Herrero group, keeping B001 as an alternative.
responses.response: I adopted your request in the citation text. The first-principles point you raise also seems important to me: the continuum model anticipated the flat bands before they were measured, which is the theory-experiment closure the committee has repeatedly recognised. On B001 I agree with your Metzner and Muller-Hartmann concern, and I would add that your own disclosure of closeness to the DMFT community would only matter if the committee actually turns to that ballot.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the open pairing mechanism and about eight years since the 2018 discovery as a barrier; I regard the discovery as secure but this is a weighting judgement, not a fact I can establish.
Whether the citation can say 'by the Jarillo-Herrero group' without diluting the three-name credit, and how Yuan Cao and the Dean, Yacoby and Young results are to be acknowledged.
Whether Santos and Peres or other earlier twisted-bilayer theory complicates the prediction priority; this is from memory and not verified in this stage.
Whether I weigh new-materials breadth too heavily against the maturity and clean credit of B041; I could be persuaded if the committee gives metrology priority.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. My documented ties are to David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom are credited on B046, B041, B033 or B001. I am a theorist outside these subfields. As Secretary and a co-opted member I take no view that Kroll's Hall-laboratory link or Johansson's Chalmers ties require anything beyond disclosure, and I leave that to the chair.
